newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Gloom over S.E Asia currencies refuses to lift.
newsitem.headline: Gloom over S.E Asia currencies refuses to lift.

text.p: Government attempts over the weekend to calm volatile markets failed to lift the gloom hanging over Southeast Asian currencies on Monday.
Dealers said the dollar was still in demand after regional currencies hit record lows on Friday following Indonesia's effective float of the rupiah.

But rather than push the dollar to new highs, players showed a greater willingness to take their profits whenever the dollar showed signs of nearing Friday's highs, although thin volumes exaggerated movements.
Dealers have lumped Southeast Asian economies together, despite hefty differences, and their negative views of the region were turned on the Philippine peso on Monday.

It fell through the 30 to the U.S. dollar level, last seen when the central bank allowed a de facto devaluation of the currency on July 11. The peso was quoted at 30.00/20 to the dollar at 0415 GMT against its previous close at 29.80.
Manila traders said the central bank was continuing to stay out of the market and quoting wide bid and offer rates of 27.00/30.15 for the dollar.
The Indonesian rupiah remained under pressure from local dollar demand in a thin market and dealers said it could test the 3,000 level.
"Volume is thin. Previously people were trading in (lots of) 10 (million dollars). Now trade volume has shrunk to one or two and sometimes five," a U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said.
The rupiah was quoted at 2,955/65 to the dollar at 0415 GMT, close to its historic low of 2,960 seen on Friday. It opened at 2,875/95.
Jakarta stocks lost over six percent in morning trade with the composite index plunging 42.71 points to 575.00 by 0350 GMT.
Dealers said the market largely ignored President Suharto's comments on Saturday that Indonesia would maintain tight monetary and fiscal policies until the rupiah stabilised.

"There are still a lot of Jakarta corporates who are short of dollars and haven't done enough hedging. The dollar is looking quite well bid at the 2,890 level for the time being," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said.

The Malaysian ringgit traded choppily, rising sharply in early trade on corporate dollar demand before slipping back as the market ignored a challenge from Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad to do its worst.
Dealers said there was little reaction to Mohamad's weekend comments that speculators were welcome to hammer down the ringgit as he was confident of overcoming the crisis.
"The market was a little surprised that nobody was willing to take the dollar higher, so they started selling it off," the U.S. bank dealer said.
"KL corporates started selling the dollar at the 2.7850 ringgit level this morning and some stop-losses were triggered on the way down," he said.
The ringgit firmed to 2.75 to the dollar from an opening around 2.78. It was quoted at 2.7745/85 at 0415 GMT.
The Singapore dollar surrendered early gains and fell back through the 1.51 level to the U.S. dollar in line with the ringgit's decline.
The Thai baht weakened towards the key 32 level versus the dollar on spillover jitters and uncertainty over the future of the Thai government after Friday's cabinet reshuffle.
The baht was quoted at 31.90/32.00 to the dollar onshore at 0415 GMT against 31.75/31.85 late on Friday.
"We have not seen any central bank intervention yet this morning. The baht's fall was capped at the 32 level," one dealer said, adding that thin volumes were exaggerating moves.
